findings.statement: The response-mapping functions produced wider error margins than the direct-mapping functions in both models.
methods: direct mapping to EQ-5D utility values by OLS regression
response mapping to EQ-5D item responses by multinomial logit

findings.statement: The EQ-5D asks about today while the SF-12 asks about the past four weeks, so haemodialysis patients surveyed during dialysis may have their quality of life overstated by the EQ-5D.

All five mapping functions were estimated on US low-income or general-population samples much younger and healthier than dialysis patients, breaking the assumption that the statistical relationship transfers.
methods: direct mapping to EQ-5D utility values by OLS regression
response mapping to EQ-5D item responses by multinomial logit

findings.statement: 356 children and adolescents were included, 181 (51%) with self-reported musculoskeletal pain; mean age 11.5 years (SD 2.9), 53% male.

EQ VAS test-retest reliability was substantial in children with musculoskeletal pain (ICC 0.81, 95% CI 0.72-0.87 for the Y-3L; 0.80, 0.71-0.86 for the Y-5L) but only moderate in those without (0.40, 0.24-0.53 and 0.58, 0.45-0.68).
Descriptive-system test-retest agreement was only fair to moderate: kappa 0.25-0.48 for the EQ-5D-Y-3L, 0.20-0.49 for the EQ-5D-Y-5L and 0.11-0.46 for the CHU9D — inadequate by COSMIN criteria.
Against the PedsQL, 89% of hypotheses were confirmed for the EQ-5D-Y-3L and 100% for the EQ-5D-Y-5L in children with musculoskeletal pain — adequate construct validity.
methods: a-priori hypothesis testing for construct validity, adequate at 75% confirmed

findings.statement: In children without musculoskeletal pain only 33% of the PedsQL hypotheses held for either EQ-5D-Y instrument, indicating inadequate construct validity in that subsample.
methods: a-priori hypothesis testing for construct validity, adequate at 75% confirmed

findings.statement: Against the CHU9D, the EQ-5D-Y-5L confirmed 81% and 75% of hypotheses in the pain and no-pain subsamples — adequate — while the EQ-5D-Y-3L reached only 44% and 69%.
methods: a-priori hypothesis testing for construct validity, adequate at 75% confirmed

findings.statement: All three instruments discriminated children with musculoskeletal pain from those without (p < 0.05) on every dimension except the EQ-5D-Y-5L 'looking after myself'.
In children with musculoskeletal pain the full-health ceiling fell from 18.2% on the EQ-5D-Y-3L to 16.0% on the EQ-5D-Y-5L; the CHU9D's all-no-problems state was reported by only 5.5%.
Completion was highest for the EQ-5D-Y-3L (98.5-98.7%) and lowest for the PedsQL (91.1-92.1%); missing data peaked at 12.7% on the EQ-5D-Y-5L 'doing usual activities' dimension.

36% of the children who reported musculoskeletal pain on the PIP-Kids reported no problems on the pain dimensions of the EQ-5D-Y instruments or CHU9D — the PIP-Kids asks about the last month, the others about today.
instruments: Presence and Impact of Pain in Kids questionnaire

findings.statement: 233 candidate severity labels were generated across the four countries, from 37 in the UK to 79 in Germany.
Each country conducted between 59 and 72 sorting and response scaling interviews, 255 in total.
methods: response scaling on a visual analogue scale
sorting task with a smiling-face scale

findings.statement: Asked directly, most participants preferred the EQ-5D-Y-5L over the 4L version — 88% in Germany, 68% in Spain and 66% in Sweden — because it let them rate their health more precisely.
methods: cognitive interview with paraphrasing and probing

findings.statement: Participants found both the 4L and 5L versions feasible to complete and easily understood; in Germany and Sweden no questions were raised about any severity label.
methods: cognitive interview with paraphrasing and probing

findings.statement: Spanish level-2 wording was changed from 'un poco de problema' to 'algún pequeño problema', and 'moderados' was replaced by 'bastante' after younger participants could not interpret it.
methods: cognitive interview with paraphrasing and probing

findings.statement: In the UK, 'terrible'/'terribly' proved problematic for primary school children as the level-5 anchor and was replaced by 'extreme'/'extremely', confirmed in four further interviews.
methods: cognitive interview with paraphrasing and probing

findings.statement: The EQ-5D-Y-5L defines 3125 possible health states against 243 for the EQ-5D-Y-3L.
Participants of all ages could rate label severity using a sorting or response scaling task — the first demonstration that response scaling is feasible in participants as young as eight.
methods: response scaling on a visual analogue scale
sorting task with a smiling-face scale

findings.statement: Pooled across 48 studies, 23% of patients reported the best health state 11111, ranging from 2% in musculoskeletal disease to 36% in cancer.
methods: random-effects meta-analysis with inverse variance weighting

findings.statement: General population studies pooled 48% at full health and healthy-population studies 41%, a substantially larger ceiling than in patient samples.
methods: random-effects meta-analysis with inverse variance weighting

findings.statement: All 17 papers reporting missing values found them under 5%, and 43 of 48 papers found the most severe health state under 15%, so the EQ-5D-5L is feasible and free from floor effects.
Of nine papers addressing test–retest reliability, eight found excellent index-level agreement and one an ICC of 0.7; five found only fair item-level agreement on some dimensions.
The EQ-5D-5L index value correlated most strongly with other multi-attribute utility instruments (pooled rho 0.756), pain/discomfort measures (0.595) and physical/functional measures (0.582).
methods: random-effects meta-analysis with inverse variance weighting

findings.statement: The EQ-5D-5L index value correlated poorly with satisfaction measures (pooled rho 0.335) and with cognition/communication measures (0.259).
methods: random-effects meta-analysis with inverse variance weighting

findings.statement: At dimension level the strongest correlation was pain/discomfort with pain measures (pooled rho 0.636); anxiety/depression was the only item correlating moderately with mental health (0.461).
Fifteen studies examined responsiveness; EQ-5D-5L index values typically showed moderate effect sizes among patients who improved, with the largest effect sizes days and weeks after giving birth.
Self-care carried a consistently large ceiling across populations, except in stroke, nervous-system and musculoskeletal patients.
The EQ-5D-5L distinguishes across disease groups, severity, symptoms, age and education, but not consistently across gender, marital status, medication frequency or health-service use.
Exploratory factor analysis loaded mobility, self-care, usual activities and pain/discomfort onto one physical factor and anxiety/depression onto a second factor with mood and confidence items.
Qualitative content-validity work found self-care too narrowly defined and usual activities too broad, with pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression judged the most relevant dimensions.
EQ-DAPHNIE targets 4500 completed responses per country across the 15 countries of rounds 1 and 2, giving a planned total of 67 500 respondents.
methods: quota sampling on age, sex and ethnicity

findings.statement: Data collection ran for six weeks per country with quota controls relaxed at five weeks, aiming for at least 85% adherence to each quota threshold.
methods: quota sampling on age, sex and ethnicity

findings.statement: The core survey administers the EQ-5D-5L and its bolt-ons alongside EQ-HWB, PROMIS-10, ASCOT or ICECAP-A, WHO-5, OPQOL-brief, PHQ-2 and GAD-2, in randomized order after the EQ-5D-5L, to support head-to-head instrument comparison.
The standardized core questionnaire takes about 20 minutes and runs to roughly 50 screens, varying slightly by country.
EQ-HWB pain severity correlated most strongly with pain frequency and with discomfort severity (both rs = 0.81), then with the EQ-5D pain/discomfort composite (0.76) and discomfort frequency (0.62).
Frequency scales were more informative than severity scales for both pain (J' 0.98 vs 0.89) and discomfort (J' 0.94 vs 0.86).
methods: Shannon's index and evenness index of scale informativity

findings.statement: EQ-HWB pain severity had the highest IRT discrimination parameter (a = 6.23) and the widest threshold range; pain frequency was more moderate (a = 3.86) with a narrower range, so severity discriminates better at high trait levels and frequency is more sensitive at low ones.
methods: item response theory graded response model

findings.statement: Total DIF between the frequency and severity scales was large for pain (ΔR² = 0.24, uniform 0.22) but negligible for discomfort (ΔR² = 0.0013).
The highest odds of reporting pain frequency were among people with immunologic conditions (OR 3.21, 95% CI 1.97-5.24) and musculoskeletal conditions (OR 2.65, 95% CI 1.95-3.61).
Depression raised the odds of reporting pain frequency (OR 1.51, 95% CI 1.08-2.11) and discomfort frequency (OR 1.50) but not their severity — the scales pick up different things.
Women were less likely than men to report pain severity (OR 0.71, 95% CI 0.56-0.90).
The EQ-5D-5L pain/discomfort composite item correlated more strongly with EQ-HWB pain measures than with discomfort measures, so it predominantly captures pain rather than discomfort.
221 codes were generated from the interviews, 34 excluded by predefined criteria, leaving 187 codes — over half of them (97) derived inductively rather than from the EQ-HWB item pool.
The 187 codes formed 57 sub-themes in eight themes: feeling and emotion, cognition, self-identity, coping, physical sensation, relationship, activity, and mindset.
The Chinese framework aligned with the EQ-HWB framework on 88% of themes (7 of 8) and 68% of sub-themes (18 of 57).

'Mindset' — life attitude, adjusting one's perspective, and positive/negative energy — emerged as a theme absent from the EQ-HWB framework, reflecting Confucian and Daoist influences on Chinese views of quality of life.
Only one EQ-HWB sub-theme, 'hearing', was absent from the Chinese framework; everything else in the EQ-HWB was reflected in it.

Two shared concepts sit under different themes in the two frameworks: 'boredom' is an emotion in the Chinese framework but an activity in the EQ-HWB, and 'sleep' an activity rather than a physical sensation.
'Positive/negative energy' and 'mindset' (心态) had no directly equivalent English connotations and were retained by character-based translation, a translation risk for adapting the EQ-HWB to China.
Data saturation was reached in the last three interviews, with similar views repeated by the last 10 interviewees, though no a priori saturation criterion was set.
44 experts were invited and 33 attended across three consultations, representing 15 countries; only five experts in paediatric instrument development took part, drawn from Europe and Canada.
The six EQ-TIPS v2.0 dimensions — movement, play, social interaction, communication, eating and pain — were judged an adequate representation of HRQoL for this age group.
Experts substantially agreed that sleep and emotions, absent from version 2.0, could be relevant and warrant testing; bowel habits attracted little support.

All three groups recommended replacing the reference to 'age-appropriate behaviour' in dimension headings with age-specific examples, to standardise interpretation across cultures and literacy levels.
Experts in all three groups questioned the overlap between the communication and social interaction dimensions and whether they could be collapsed into one; no consensus was reached.

Proxy completion was held to introduce subjectivity from intrinsic factors (age, personal experience, number of children) and extrinsic ones (social support, resource access), with the ideal proxy depending on context — clinicians for hospitalised children.
Several experts were unsure whether EQ-TIPS measures health, health status, HRQoL or development, and asked for a stated definition to guide users.

Experts warned that dimensions must stay on the child's health rather than its impact on the family, or EQ-TIPS will incidentally capture caregiver spillover — the eating and sleeping dimensions being most at risk.
The movement dimension was flagged as a translation risk: the commonest Chinese term denotes walking, while the dimension covers rolling and crawling too.
'Today' was generally endorsed as the recall period, optimal for acute conditions and repeated measures, though some experts wanted a longer window for chronic or fluctuating conditions.

The instrument's deficit focus on problems rather than abilities was called ableist, though experts acknowledged it is common to HRQoL instruments and may be needed to measure responsiveness in trials.
The Danish EQ-5D-5L value set has its lowest value, − 0.757, at health state 55555.
methods: hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data

findings.statement: 21.7% of the 3125 health states in the Danish EQ-5D-5L value set are valued worse than dead, against 19.75% for the 3L and 11.01% for the crosswalk value set.
22% of the observed cTTO values were for states considered worse than death, and observed cTTO values ranged from 1 to − 1.
Mean self-reported EQ VAS in the Danish valuation sample was 82.4 (SD 15.9).

Anxiety/depression carried the largest utility decrement in the Danish 5L value set, followed by pain/discomfort and then mobility — a reordering relative to the Danish 3L value set, where mobility ranked first.
Only the heteroscedastic censored hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data produced logically consistent parameter estimates; the cTTO-only and DCE-only models each left inconsistent parameters.
methods: hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data

findings.statement: Only seven respondents (0.7%) in the Danish sample were non-traders, against nearly 14% in the French valuation study.

The valuation sample matched the Danish adult general population on gender, age, marital status and region, but over-represented respondents with higher education and under-represented 18–24 year olds.
1476 individuals took part: 1058 in the DCE interviews and 418 in the cTTO interviews, quota sampled to be representative of the Chinese general population.
methods: quota sampling on age, sex and ethnicity

findings.statement: The highest observed mean cTTO value was 0.924 (SE 0.011) for state 11112 and the lowest was − 0.088 (SE 0.025) for state 33333, the only state with a negative observed mean.
21.89% of cTTO observations (n = 915) were negative, with values concentrated at the upper end of the scale and only a 1.65% spike at − 1.0.
The hybrid model with an A3 term gave the lowest mean absolute error (0.030) with no inconsistent or non-significant coefficients, and was selected as the value set.
methods: hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data
anchoring DCE latent values by regression onto observed cTTO values
mixed logit model with correlated random coefficients

findings.statement: A value gap of about 0.31 separated state 33333 (− 0.088) from the second worst state 33323 (0.219), the same discontinuity reported in other EQ-5D-Y-3L valuation studies.
Pain/discomfort was the most important dimension and mobility and self-care the least, reversing the ordering in the Chinese EQ-5D-3L and EQ-5D-5L value sets where mobility ranked first.
methods: hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data

findings.statement: Values for state 33333 are markedly higher in Asian countries (China − 0.088, Japan 0.200, Indonesia − 0.086) than in European ones (Slovenia − 0.691, Spain − 0.389, Hungary − 0.517, Netherlands − 0.372, Germany − 0.260).
cTTO interviews took 35.70 minutes on average (SD 12.42) with 13.21 moves (SD 9.00); DCE interviews averaged 9.61 minutes (SD 7.12).
The EQ-5D-5L ceiling was 41%, and 77% of respondents at 11111 reported problems on at least one bolt-on item.
Adding sleep or self-confidence cut the EQ-5D-5L ceiling by 30%, tiredness by 24% and vision by 21%; further bolt-ons added little beyond the second.
Bolt-on ceilings ranged from 38% for tiredness to 81% for breathing; sleep, tiredness and vision all had lower ceilings than any EQ-5D-5L dimension, and floors were under 2% throughout.

Breathing, hearing and vision correlated only weakly with every EQ-5D-5L item, so they cover ground the core five do not; skin irritation was also only weakly correlated with pain/discomfort, against expectation.
Tiredness correlated moderately with both pain/discomfort (0.47) and anxiety/depression (0.50), and cognition, self-confidence and social relationships correlated moderately with anxiety/depression.
All bolt-ons except cognition and self-confidence loaded on a factor distinct from the EQ-5D-5L dimensions; the cognition bolt-on loaded with psychological functioning rather than a cognitive factor.
methods: confirmatory factor analysis with diagonally weighted least squares
principal component analysis with promax rotation

findings.statement: Bolt-ons raised the EQ-5D-5L's ability to separate people with chronic conditions from healthy respondents, with relative efficiencies from 1.09 (95% CI 1.03-1.17) to 1.95 (1.68-2.41).
methods: EQ-5D-5L level sum score, transformed to a 0-100 scale
relative efficiency as the ratio of ANOVA F-statistics, bootstrapped CIs

findings.statement: The sleep bolt-on made the largest contribution to known-group validity in 9 of 13 chronic conditions, physical and mental alike.
methods: relative efficiency as the ratio of ANOVA F-statistics, bootstrapped CIs

findings.statement: Tiredness explained the most EQ VAS variance in 8 of 13 conditions; with the five EQ-5D-5L items alone, adjusted R² was 0.44 for EQ VAS, 0.52 for PROMIS Global Health and 0.24 for the Satisfaction with Life Scale, and bolt-ons raised these only modestly.
methods: univariable and multivariable linear regression of explanatory power

findings.statement: Problems on breathing, hearing, skin irritation, sleep and vision rose with age while self-confidence and social relationships fell (P < .05); hearing and vision were the most effective at capturing declining health with age.
The EQ-5D-5L produced 203 distinct health profiles (7% of those possible) with the 20 commonest covering 79.3% of the sample; adding bolt-ons increased profile diversity and spread respondents out.
Only 9.45% reported no problems on all EQ-HWB-S dimensions against 36.04% on the EQ-5D-5L, and nobody reported the worst state on either instrument.
EQ-HWB-S mobility was the only dimension over the 70% ceiling threshold (83%); EQ-5D-5L self-care reached 90.99% and mobility 78.58%.
Fewer respondents reported no problems on the EQ-HWB-S anxiety (43%) and sadness/depression (55%) items than on the combined EQ-5D-5L anxiety/depression dimension (58%).

All correlations between conceptually overlapping dimensions of the two instruments were strong (rs ≥ 0.5), and the EQ-HWB-S utility score correlated 0.507 to 0.624 with EQ-5D-5L dimensions — except self-care, at −0.440.
The EQ-HWB-S wellbeing items — exhaustion, loneliness and cognition — correlated only weakly to moderately (0.151-0.495) with EQ-5D-5L items, so they capture ground the EQ-5D-5L does not.

Lin's concordance correlation coefficient between the two utility scores was 0.848 — excellent concordance — though utility differences ranged from −0.61 to 0.31 with a mean absolute difference of 0.17.

Large effect sizes (≥0.8) separated healthy from unhealthy respondents, those with and without a long-term condition, and above from below average health and life satisfaction — and employed from unemployed or long-term sick.
methods: Cohen's d effect size for known-group differences

findings.statement: Effect sizes were only small for distinguishing carers from non-carers and across age groups, and differed only minorly between the EQ-HWB-S and EQ-5D-5L throughout.
methods: Cohen's d effect size for known-group differences

findings.statement: EQ-HWB-S utilities ran from −0.212 to 1 (SD 0.20) and mapped EQ-5D-5L utilities from −0.25 to 0.988 (SD 0.19); mean EQ VAS was 76 (SD 17.54).
methods: NICE-recommended mapping of EQ-5D-5L responses onto the EQ-5D-3L UK value set

findings.statement: Fewer than 5% of respondents reached the worst level on any dimension of either instrument; exhaustion had the highest floor at 4%, and EQ-HWB-S mobility and EQ-5D-5L self-care had none.
Values from the nonlinear DCEd model correlated 0.954 with modelled cTTO values, 0.973 with the rescaled EQ-VT mixed logit and 0.973 with the hybrid models across all 3125 health states.
methods: discrete choice experiment with a duration attribute, split-triplet design
hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data
mixed logit model with correlated random coefficients

findings.statement: Mean absolute differences between DCEd and the three EQ-VT models were 0.083, 0.051 and 0.060 — comparable to the 0.045 between cTTO and latent-scale DCE collected in the same sample.
methods: discrete choice experiment with a duration attribute, split-triplet design

findings.statement: State 55555 was valued at −0.543 by the nonlinear DCEd model against −0.611, −0.686 and −0.563 by the three EQ-VT models; the linear DCEd model gave an implausible −1.214.
methods: discrete choice experiment with a duration attribute, split-triplet design
exponential discounting correction for nonlinear time preferences

findings.statement: Pain/discomfort level 5 carried the largest weight in every EQ-VT model (0.464 to 0.541) with mobility second; the nonlinear DCEd model put pain/discomfort marginally ahead of mobility (−0.365 vs −0.361).
methods: discrete choice experiment with a duration attribute, split-triplet design
hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data

findings.statement: An annual discount rate of 23.5% (95% CI 21.7%-25.3%) best described the DCEd data, higher than the 17.3% reported for the same method applied to the Well-being of Older People instrument.
methods: discrete choice experiment with a duration attribute, split-triplet design
exponential discounting correction for nonlinear time preferences

findings.statement: 611 of 1581 DCEd respondents (38.6%) failed quality control; 62.46% of those recruited in public places were speeders and 74.6% flatlined, so that entire recruitment mode was discarded.
methods: discrete choice experiment with a duration attribute, split-triplet design

findings.statement: 61.7% of excluded respondents always chose the same option in the B/C comparison, against 22.4% of those retained — the method cannot distinguish flatlining from a genuine strong preference.
methods: discrete choice experiment with a duration attribute, split-triplet design

findings.statement: Against the mean observed cTTO values for the 86 design states, mean absolute error was 0.081 for DCEd, 0.042 for cTTO, 0.053 for the rescaled DCE and 0.044 for the hybrid model.
methods: discrete choice experiment with a duration attribute, split-triplet design
hybrid model combining cTTO and DCE data

findings.statement: Predicted values ranged from − 0.654 for the worst health state 55555 to 0.962 for 11211, with 15.3% of predicted values worse than dead.
methods: hybrid tobit model censored at -1 correcting for heteroskedasticity

findings.statement: Mobility had the largest impact on health state values, followed by pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression, then self-care and usual activities.
methods: hybrid tobit model censored at -1 correcting for heteroskedasticity

findings.statement: 25.7% of observed cTTO valuations were worse than dead, and the mean observed value was negative for 11 of the 86 design states.
The mean observed cTTO value across the 86 health states was 0.303 (SD 0.657), from − 0.538 for 55555 to 0.948 for the very mild states.
34.5% of UAE respondents reported mild to severe problems in pain/discomfort and 32.5% in anxiety/depression, against 9.9% in mobility and 2.6% in self-care; mean EQ VAS was 86.0 (SD 11.4).
285 participants (28.4%) had at least one valuation inconsistency, falling to 160 (15.9%) after the feedback module; 10.1% of cTTO responses were flagged.
Of 14 trained interviewers, five were not allowed to collect data because of significant data-quality concerns and two dropped out, leaving seven.
The UAE value of − 0.654 for 55555 is close to Saudi Arabia's (− 0.683), above Egypt's (− 0.964) and below the United States' (− 0.573).
Data quality differences between Arabic and English and between in-person and online interviews were minimal, so all data were combined — supporting online interviewing for valuation studies.
2125 unique RCTs met the eligibility criteria out of 11 633 records identified.
Only 6.2% of trials measured the EQ-5D as a primary outcome; it was a secondary outcome in 57.4% and exploratory in 36.5%.
EQ-5D utilities were the most analysed data type (74.9% of trials), ahead of EQ VAS (56.3%) and dimension responses (18.1%).
For single post-baseline utility the linear fixed-effect model was most used (192 of 589, 32.6%); for multiple post-baselines it was the linear mixed-effect model (338 of 984, 34.3%).
methods: linear fixed-effect model (including ANCOVA and multiple linear regression)
linear mixed-effect model (multilevel or hierarchical model)

findings.statement: Of the 2054 trials analysing numerical EQ-5D data, only 10.8% reported examining model assumptions and 21.3% adjusted for the baseline score; just 2.6% used a minimal important difference to interpret the treatment effect.
methods: linear fixed-effect model (including ANCOVA and multiple linear regression)

findings.statement: Missing EQ-5D data were explicitly examined in only 31.1% of trials, and of those just over half imputed — most often by multiple imputation (200) or last observation carried forward (106).
Utilities and EQ VAS were analysed almost entirely in their original numerical format (98.8% and 99.1%); dimension responses were mostly categorical (60.0%).
The five commonest therapeutic areas were orthopedics (16.4%), cardiology (13.9%), oncology (12.5%), psychiatry (8.1%) and rheumatology (7.6%).
EQ-5D utilities and EQ VAS are skewed, ceilinged and discrete, breaking the normality assumption of the linear regressions the field mostly uses, yet few studies checked those assumptions.
methods: linear fixed-effect model (including ANCOVA and multiple linear regression)

findings.statement: 238 individuals from 45 countries and 65 HTA agencies completed the survey, a mean of 5.28 responses per country (SD 4.45).
The three most frequently used utility instruments among HTA practitioners doing QALY-related work were EQ-5D ("very often"), SF-6D ("occasionally") and EQ-5D-Y ("occasionally").
Time trade-off, visual analogue scale and standard gamble were the three most frequently used elicitation methods, all rated "often"; DCE was only "occasionally" used in most regions.
87.7% of respondents agreed the choice of utility instrument matters, from 66.7% in the Middle East/Africa to 91.2% in Western Europe.
79.8% of respondents agreed the choice of elicitation method matters, from 69.6% in East and Central Europe to 86.7% in Western Europe.
91.2% of respondents agreed the health preference data source matters, and the general public of another country was used more frequently than the local public.

Poor sample representativeness, small sample size, mismatch between available health states and the CEA model, and mixing elicitation methods within one model were all "often" encountered; outdated data was less of a concern.

Globally the top research priority was making more recent utility values available (importance score 0.20), ahead of instruments for children and adolescents (0.19) and instruments capturing both healthcare and social care (0.17).

Social care was the top-voted priority in Asia (0.21) and Western Europe (0.33); recent tariffs led in the Middle East/Africa (0.33) and Central/Eastern Europe (0.31); carers led in the Commonwealth (0.23) and care inequality in Latin America (0.22).

Respondents' main criticism of the EQ-5D was poor responsiveness in certain health conditions, and of the TTO its high cognitive burden; those respondents had not considered EQ-HWB, PROPr, bolt-ons or DCE as alternatives.

Of 144 qualitative responses, 81 held that the general public's preferences should determine utility values against 53 for patients' preferences, and 79 said preferences should come from one's own country.
methods: content analysis of interview transcripts with an emergent code book

findings.statement: The EQ-5D-5L index correlated strongly and negatively with the ThyPRO-39 composite score (-0.567) and moderately with the overall QoL-impact score (-0.350); EQ VAS correlated -0.483 and -0.451 respectively.
One-month agreement was highest for self-care (Gwet's AC2 0.964) and lowest for anxiety/depression (0.788), with percentage agreement running from 0.967 down to 0.882.
methods: Gwet's agreement coefficient 2 for ordinal variables

findings.statement: Test-retest ICC was 0.707 for the EQ-5D-5L index and 0.700 for the EQ VAS — moderate reliability.
Among patients reporting worsened health at six months, SES and SRM were -0.66 and -0.42 for the EQ-5D-5L index and -1.15 and -1.00 for the EQ VAS — the index fell 0.05 (0.92 to 0.87, P = 0.027).
In patients reporting improved health the instrument was not responsive: SES -0.16 and SRM -0.17 for the index, 0.19 and 0.20 for the EQ VAS, neither change significant.
28.0% of patients reported the perfect health state 11111 at baseline — a ceiling effect that leaves the index unable to register improvement — against 5.6% at the top of the EQ VAS.
Best-level responses ran from 94.4% on self-care and 88.0% on mobility down to 55.2% on pain/discomfort and 46.4% on anxiety/depression.
Mean EQ-5D-5L index was 0.91 (SD 0.10) at baseline, 0.88 at one month and 0.90 at six months; mean EQ VAS was 79.16, 78.91 and 77.95.
The 0.05 reduction seen in patients reporting worsened health matches a published minimal clinically important difference for the EQ-5D-5L of 0.058 (SD 0.005).
Eight children ranked five severity cards across four dimensions, 160 rankings in all; 10 (6.25%) were misordered, four of them by a single child.
methods: card ranking exercise for severity qualifiers

findings.statement: Children took a mean 5.2 minutes (SD 2.18) to self-complete the Arabic EQ-5D-Y-5L, and all but one found it clear, easy and not too long.

Even with 'in my body' added to the dimension name, some children gave psychological examples for 'having pain or discomfort', so the Arabic term for pain was replaced with one that refers to physical pain.

Five of eleven children did not understand the Arabic word chosen for 'item' in the digital version's blank-response prompt; four proposed 'question', which was adopted and confirmed in three further interviews.
Back translation required only one change to the first Arabic consensus version — the digital source's word for 'item', which came back as 'element' and 'value'.
methods: dual independent back translation by native speakers of the source language

findings.statement: Children over 11 had no trouble with the instructions while 8-11 year olds needed to read them twice or seek confirmation, leading the authors to recommend the interviewer-administered version for ages 8-10.
The literal Arabic equivalents of 'quite', 'really' and 'extremely' were rejected as indistinguishable for this age group in favour of simpler words that separate the severity grades more visibly.
methods: dual independent forward translation with reconciliation

findings.statement: Three of eight Egyptian children inverted severity qualifiers in the ranking exercise, in line with three of nine in South Africa and two of ten in Indonesia.
methods: card ranking exercise for severity qualifiers

findings.statement: The transformed level sum score was highest in Italy (mean 90.7, SD 11.8) and lowest in the UK (84.8, SD 18.9); EQ VAS followed the same order at 77.6 and 71.4.
methods: EQ-5D-5L level sum score, transformed to a 0-100 scale

findings.statement: In the UK and the Netherlands the level sum score was worst for respondents with low education and better at middle and high levels; in Italy the middle-education group scored best.

findings.statement: 103 of 170 eligible consenting patients (60.6%) completed at least one follow-up questionnaire within an eight-month accrual period; 22.3% of those completed three or more follow-ups.

findings.statement: Asked whether they would keep answering EQ-5D questions at each clinic visit, 115 patients (71.9%) said definitely and 35 (21.9%) very likely; nobody answered 'very unlikely' or 'definitely not'.
methods: descriptive feasibility statistics: completion and willingness rates

findings.statement: 80.0% strongly agreed the EQ-5D-3L instructions and questions were easy to understand and 83.1% that it was easy to complete; only one patient (0.6%) strongly disagreed on comprehension.

findings.statement: Administering the questionnaire during chemotherapy gave patients time to answer but exposed responses to moment-to-moment changes in treatment; patients called the day of chemotherapy an inadequate snapshot of their HRQoL.
